title: Extending LLDB to Debug Applications That Span CPUs and GPUs
abstract: We built a vendor-neutral accelerator plugin architecture in lldb-server for debugging applications that span CPUs and GPUs. It separates shared debugger infrastructure from hardware-specific device control. The design represents the CPU and GPU as separate debugger processes while presenting them in one debugging session. Modern AI applications rarely execute in one place. A workload can begin in a high-level framework and move back and forth between native CPU code and kernels running on a GPU. When a bug crosses those boundaries, developers need to understand the host application and the device together. That is harder than attaching a conventional debugger to another process. The CPU and GPU may use different instruction sets, registers, memory spaces, and execution models. The GPU is also controlled through a runtime and driver inside the host process, so debugging the device often requires careful coordination with the CPU. Historically, GPU vendors built device-specific debuggers, including AMD’s ROCgdb and NVIDIA’s CUDA-GDB. These tools provide deep support for their respective platforms, but common debugger capabilities must often be implemented and maintained separately. At Meta, we have been developing a different approach for LLDB: a common accelerator plugin architecture in lldb-server . In this post, “GPU” refers to the concrete devices and examples, while “accelerator” refers to LLDB’s broader, vendor-neutral plugin abstraction. The architecture has evolved through contributions from engineers at Meta and across the accelerator ecosystem. It keeps the shared debugger independent of any one GPU while giving hardware vendors a focused place to implement device-specific behavior. Why GPU Debugging Challenges Traditional Debugger Models A traditional debugger generally assumes that one process has one architecture and a consistent view of threads, registers, and memory. GPU programs challenge each of those assumptions. A host process might run on x86-64 while its kernels use a completely different instruction set. A CPU thread has a familiar register context, while a GPU may execute groups of lanes in lockstep. Host and device pointers can refer to different address spaces. A GPU can expose thousands of execution lanes, which do not map cleanly onto the thread model that most command-line and graphical debuggers present. Combining all of this state into one artificial process model makes the debugger more complicated. Every operation must first determine whether it applies to the CPU or the GPU. Register handling, memory reads, breakpoints, stepping, and stop events all become conditional on the selected hardware. A single process model also forces the CPU and GPU into one unified memory map, even though their address spaces can be independent: The same address, such as 0x1000, can refer to different locations in the CPU and GPU processes. Instead of hiding those differences, the LLDB accelerator architecture gives them a clear boundary. Plugin Support in lldb-server for GPU Debugging LLDB uses a companion process called lldb-server to launch or attach to a program and perform low-level debugging operations. The LLDB client communicates with the server through the GDB remote protocol, a command protocol for operations such as reading memory, inspecting registers, controlling execution, and setting breakpoints. Because lldb-server already controls the native process, it is also the right place to coordinate with an accelerator runtime. The new plugin interface lets a hardware-specific backend work alongside the normal CPU debugger. The backend translates a vendor’s device debugging API into concepts LLDB already understands, such as processes, threads, registers, memory, modules, and stop reasons. This separation keeps the LLDB client vendor-neutral. Common improvements to the command line, remote protocol, symbol handling, and IDE integration can benefit every accelerator. title: How skills and agents work in AWS Quick
abstract: If you use AI agents, you’ve probably explained the same task more than once. You might describe how to build your weekly status update, write release notes, manage a project, or create tickets. These are all repeatable tasks that you can encode using AWS Quick through agents and skills. AWS Quick is an AI-powered service for automating tasks, analyzing data, building web applications, and conducting research. You work with it in natural language, and Quick uses AI agents to process your requests against your connected data sources and applications. In this post, we cover how agents, skills, and your data fit together in AWS Quick, and how to build and share skills that work for your team. We also show how the official catalog and custom agents help you put those skills to use. Understanding foundational concepts In this section, we explain the foundational concepts that help you understand AWS Quick in relation to agents, skills, and your data. Figure 1: How a Quick agent follows its instructions, loads the skills a task needs, acts through connectors, and grounds its answers in your data The agent sits at the center of Figure 1. It follows its instructions, loads the skills that a task calls for, takes action through connectors, and grounds its answers in your data: spaces, knowledge bases, datasets, and dashboards. Working with agents An agent in AWS Quick is a configurable AI with its own instructions, knowledge sources (spaces), and connectors, which it uses to answer questions and get work done for you. You can work with an agent in chat, or let it run on its own using a routine . Agents can only reach the resources and services that you can, and you decide what each agent is allowed to do. Quick is the default built-in agent that every user has access to. It has no fixed scope, so in each conversation it works with whatever resources you have access to, such as your spaces, knowledge bases, dashboards, connectors, and skills. You don’t need to decide in advance which data or tools a request needs, so you can start most work with Quick. A custom agent is one that you or someone on your team configures for a specific job. An example is a human resources (HR) onboarding assistant that answers new-hire questions from the HR team’s space. You give it its own instructions and limit it to the spaces, connectors, and skills that your use case requires. After you test and publish it, you can share it with other users and groups within your AWS Quick account. For a walkthrough of building one, see Build AI-powered employee onboarding agents with AWS Quick . Working with data Agents ground their answers in the data you connect to Quick. A space is a curated collection of documents and AWS Quick resources that an agent uses as a source of information. You can create one for yourself, your team, or another group in your organization. You can upload files and folders to a space, or add assets such as dashboards, knowledge bases, action connectors, and datasets. When you start a conversation with Quick, you can attach a space to narrow the data that Quick uses for that conversation. When you add a space to an agent, the space becomes part of the agent’s configuration, and the agent draws on it when a request needs it. A knowledge base is an organized, indexed collection of documents or content from data sources, optimized for retrieval and question answering. Quick syncs knowledge bases from sources such as Google Drive, Microsoft OneDrive, Confluence, Microsoft SharePoint, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), web crawler, or Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases . Quick keeps them up to date on a sync schedule. Datasets and dashboards come from AWS Quick Sight , the business intelligence feature in Quick, which is available in accounts provisioned through the AWS Management Console. title: Single-shot and agentic retrieval with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base
abstract: A banking operations employee starts the morning by asking an internal AI assistant which documents are needed to open a business account. The answer is in a single checklist. A few hours later, the same employee asks how those requirements differ across sole proprietorships, LLCs, and partnerships with multiple owners. That answer is spread across several policy guides. One assistant has to handle both questions, quickly and cheaply for the first and thoroughly for the second. Applications need a way to match retrieval effort to each request without building separate systems for simple and complex questions. Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base now supports single-shot Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and retrieval-only requests through AgenticRetrieveStream . With single-shot RAG, the service searches your knowledge bases once and uses a foundation model (FM) to generate an answer from the passages it finds. With retrieval-only requests, the service returns the matching passages without generating an answer, so your application or the user can work with the source text directly. These modes join the existing agentic retrieval, where the service plans and runs multiple searches before answering. You can now use the same API for both of the employee’s questions: single-shot RAG for the checklist lookup and agentic retrieval for the cross-policy comparison. In this post, we explain how the new settings work and when to use each mode. We use an illustrative internal banking policy assistant to show how single-shot RAG handles direct questions and how agentic retrieval supports comparisons across policy documents. We also show how to configure retrieval-only requests when an employee needs to review source passages rather than a generated answer. Key benefits Agentic retrieval helps an assistant answer questions that require more than one search. A foundation model breaks the question into sub-queries, searches the relevant knowledge bases, and evaluates whether the results provide enough information to answer the original question. If it identifies gaps, it can refine the search and retrieve additional evidence, within the configured iteration limit. For application builders, this provides several benefits: Better support for multi-part questions – Targeted searches can find evidence for each part of a question instead of relying on one search to cover everything. In the banking example, the assistant can look up requirements for sole proprietors and LLCs separately before comparing them. Follow-up searches when information is missing – The planner can use what it finds to decide what to search for next. It can also retrieve a full document when a passage doesn’t provide enough context, helping address gaps that a single retrieval might leave unresolved. Answers with supporting evidence – When response generation is enabled, the service combines retrieved information into an answer with citations. Trace events show the planning and retrieval steps, helping developers inspect how the answer was produced. Less custom orchestration – The service manages the planning, retrieval, evaluation, and response-generation workflow through one API. Applications don’t need to implement their own loop to coordinate these steps. These agentic capabilities remain valuable for complex questions. For straightforward lookups, applications also need a way to retrieve and answer without additional planning. The expanded maxAgentIteration range closes that gap. With one parameter, you can choose one of three modes for each request: Retrieval-only returns passages without generating an answer. Single-shot RAG retrieves once and generates an answer, with no planning rounds. Agentic retrieval plans and runs multiple searches for complex questions. Single-shot RAG uses one foundation model call to generate the answer, which can reduce latency and model usage compared with agentic retrieval. title: Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 on AWS
abstract: Today, we are announcing the availability of Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on Amazon Bedrock and Claude Platform on AWS. Claude Fable 5.2 is Anthropic’s most capable generally available model for technical work that raises the bar in coding and the sciences. Claude Mythos 5.2 is available through Anthropic’s verification programs for advanced work in cyber security and life sciences. In this post, we cover what’s new in both models, why Fable 5.2 matters for your technical workloads, and how to get started building with the model on Amazon Bedrock. Why Claude Fable 5.2 Fable 5.2 raises the bar on the hardest problems in coding, math, and science. It takes on ambiguous, multi-step work, verifies its own output, and can run unattended for hours to days. It interprets prompts, iterates, catches its own errors, and optimizes as it goes. In Anthropic’s alignment testing, Mythos 5.2 hallucinates less, completes tasks more reliably, surfaces important information more consistently, and self-reports issues more honestly than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1. Anthropic expects Fable 5.2 to behave similarly. If a cyber security query is declined, you can retry it on Opus 4.8, and if a biology query is declined, you can retry it on Opus 5. On Amazon Bedrock, the retry is your code’s job, not an automatic switch. If the declined request hit the prompt cache, the refusal also includes a fallback credit token. Send that token with the retry and it’s billed as cache reads, so you don’t pay to write the same cache twice. Check the documentation for more information on fallback credit. For authorized work in cyber security and life sciences, Claude Mythos 5.2 is available through Anthropic’s verification programs . Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 use cases Where Fable 5.2 fits: Agentic coding across large, multi-repository codebases. Long-running agents for coordinating many subagents on multi-day work. Scientific research from new analytical methods to formal mathematical proofs. Financial analysis for quantitative research and forecasting. Design for 3D, hardware, and motion for generating environments, components, and simulations in code. Mythos 5.2 covers two high-risk domains, available only through the verification programs noted earlier: Cyber security , for security engineering, red teaming, and penetration testing. Life sciences research , especially biomolecular design and research synthesis. Data retention and Enterprise Frontier Safeguards Anthropic designates Claude Fable 5.2 as a Covered Model . By default, its use requires retention for up to 30 days and human safety review. On Amazon Bedrock, Amazon personnel perform the review within the AWS boundary. Set the aws_review data retention mode on your account or project before you invoke the model. See Amazon Bedrock data retention for more details. Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS), built in collaboration with AWS, combines the privacy of zero data retention (ZDR) with state-of-the-art safeguards for detecting misuse. EFS works by storing data in cloud infrastructure controlled by the customer. Until EFS is available, eligible customers can use Fable 5.2 with zero data retention. This is available for internal use through at least June 30, 2027. Getting started with Claude Fable 5.2 on Amazon Bedrock To try Fable 5.2, open the Amazon Bedrock console , choose Test , Playground , and select Fable 5.2 as the model. title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
abstract: Today, we’re announcing that NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. You can deploy it with a few steps in SageMaker Studio or with a few lines of the SageMaker Python SDK. Super VL is the vision-language model (VLM) in the NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 family. It accepts images, video, and text as input and generates text. The model pairs a 120B-parameter hybrid Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language backbone with 12B active parameters and a C-RADIO vision encoder. It supports context lengths of up to 1 million tokens and includes a built-in Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) head that supports speculative decoding. You can configure reasoning per request. NVIDIA built Super VL for document intelligence, GUI understanding for computer-use agents, video question answering, and multimodal agentic applications. JumpStart offers two variants: NVFP4, quantized from BF16 with quantization-aware distillation for optimized inference, and the BF16 full-precision reference weights. In this post, we walk through the model’s capabilities and the JumpStart deployment configurations. We then show the measured inference performance and demonstrate text, image, and video inference. Model overview Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a 120B-parameter model with 12B active parameters per token. It combines a hybrid language backbone with a dedicated vision encoder. Language backbone : 88 layers that interleave Mamba-2 and MoE layers (512 routed experts, 22 active per token) with 8 attention layers, plus a shared MTP head. The backbone is initialized from Nemotron 3 Super Base and distilled from Nemotron 3 Ultra Base. Vision encoder : A C-RADIO vision encoder encodes images and sampled video frames, and a vision-language connector maps them into the language backbone’s embedding space. The encoder and connector stay in BF16 in both variants. Training : The model first goes through continued pre-training, long-context and software-engineering mid-training, and vision-language training. It then goes through two-stage multimodal supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on vision, reasoning, code, tool, chat, safety, and long-context data. Next come reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards and human feedback in NeMo RL and NeMo Gym, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and a final stage that further trains the MTP head. The NVFP4 checkpoint is produced from BF16 with NVIDIA Model Optimizer and quantization-aware distillation. It keeps the vision encoder, connector, Mamba convolutions, and embeddings in BF16 and the MoE router in FP32. It runs with 4-bit weights and activations (W4A4) on Blackwell GPUs. title: Pluggable Agentic AI Framework: A seven-layer composable enterprise agentic AI reference architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: “How do we run our AI agents in production at scale?” is the question every customer eventually asks. It comes bundled with several questions. How do we handle thousands of concurrent user requests securely and confidently? How do we make sure the agents stay reliable under real traffic instead of failing silently? How do we know if an agent still meets the quality and safety standards it passed during testing? What are agent security best practices? Should that be deterministic or non-deterministic? And many more. A proof-of-concept answers none of these, because it is built to show the agent model can do the task, not to survive production traffic, cost pressure, and security review. That gap between a working prototype and a system that runs reliably, securely, frugally and responsibly at scale, is where most agentic AI initiatives stall, and it is rarely the model’s fault. Every team building an agent tends to rebuild the same scaffolding from scratch: its own routing logic, its own guardrails, its own observability, all applied after the fact rather than built in from the start. The teams need a shared, production-ready architecture that every agent can build on. This post walks through a seven-layer composable reference architecture designed to take multi-agent AI applications from prototype to production scale. Composable architecture The Pluggable Agentic AI Framework is a reference architecture for multi-agent applications organized into seven layers , each with a distinct responsibility and a stable contract. The services and technologies shown in each layer reflect the reference implementation, not mandatory choices. Organizations can substitute alternatives that align with their existing infrastructure and requirements. Together, these layers offer a blueprint for building, securing, and operating agentic AI applications at production scale. Figure 1: The seven layers of the Pluggable Agentic AI Framework Data and Knowledge is the foundation of Agentic AI. An agent is only as good as the data it can access. Whether an agent is checking out a healthcare formulary, tracking inventory, or interpreting a compliance rule, it needs relevant, up-to-date information to answer correctly. This layer owns retrieval, embeddings, and access to structured and unstructured data through a clear contract and protocol: accept a query and return the most relevant information that acts as context for an agent. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base , Vector Engine for Amazon OpenSearch Serverless , Amazon S3 Vectors and Amazon DynamoDB are example building blocks for this foundation. Model and Inference choices should be driven by configuration, not hardwired into agent or application logic. Use smaller, faster models for simple tasks and larger models for requests that require more nuanced reasoning. It is important to conduct a thorough model evaluation for the use case you are building with realistic and representative business data. A model routing layer keeps AI agents decoupled from the model hosting environment and provider-specific APIs by relying on a consistent request-and-response contract. A proxy such as LiteLLM provides a common interface across providers, so you can switch models based on your evaluations without rewriting application logic. Orchestration determines how work is distributed, and choosing the right approach is critical. For straightforward tasks, use a single agent to handle the work from end to end. For complex, cross-domain workflows, use a supervisor to delegate specialist agents, each scoped to a specific capability and tied to a specific set of tools. Avoid building one agent that does everything. As tools, instructions, and context accumulate, the context window grows, latency increases, and accuracy can suffer. Tool sprawl sets in, which can push agents beyond their intended boundaries, leading to unintended actions and security breaches. title: How CrossnoKaye grounds physical AI with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: Industrial operations present AI challenges that don’t show up in typical enterprise software. In most facilities, plant data and control logic are spread across separate systems from different vendors: programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and distributed control systems (DCS) run the equipment logic, historians record time-series tags under site-specific naming schemes, supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems drive operator screens, and standalone optimization tools or alarm loggers sit on the side. Bolting an external AI agent onto that stack rarely works well in practice. Each system uses its own naming conventions. The logic that actually governs how equipment behaves (the control sequences, state machines, and safety interlocks) is locked inside proprietary controller code that an external tool can’t inspect. Giving a bolt-on agent access across multiple operational technology (OT) systems also means distributing credentials across the plant network. CrossnoKaye took a different approach to bring physical AI to heavy industry using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore . Its software-defined automation platform, ATLAS, connects live plant data and AI reasoning to closed-loop control of the equipment running food and beverage plants, industrial refrigeration facilities, aggregates quarries, and manufacturing sites. Across more than 100 industrial facilities and 13,000 controlled assets, CrossnoKaye stores over 22 trillion machine data points, ingests more than 50 billion new readings every day, and runs over 1,000 live advanced process control (APC) applications; CrossnoKaye reports that these applications improve production throughput by 11–17 percent while reducing total facility energy costs by an average of 21 percent. Because ATLAS already manages the facility model, the base control software, the historian, and the optimization applications in one platform on AWS, CrossnoKaye’s agentic intelligence system, AURA, has native access to the full operational state of the plant within a single security boundary. Having the plant context is only half the problem, though. Large language models (LLMs) are good at interpreting engineering context and planning an investigation, but they cannot reliably compute statistics or physical balances over millions of sensor readings in a prompt. To back every numerical answer with real math, AURA uses the code interpreter capability in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to write and run Python workloads at runtime inside isolated, AWS managed microVM sandboxes, alongside Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and local edge safety controls. This post covers how CrossnoKaye architected ATLAS and AURA on AWS, how AURA uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore across interactive Chats, repeatable Tasks, and automated Routines, and what the team learned running physical AI in production. Solution overview ATLAS controls industrial processes across existing PLC and DCS infrastructure, from kilns, crushers, drying rooms, ovens, and spiral freezers to chillers, turbines, valves, and compressors, without requiring customers to rip and replace plant hardware. title: Fact-Checking at Scale: Building a More Accurate and Efficient Synopsis Factuality System
abstract: By Shreya S Ramanujam , Yongce Li , Afshine Amidi , Sina Ghiassian , Benjamin Klein . Introduction Picture this — you’re home after a long day at work and can’t wait to catch up on Bridgerton. You log on to Netflix, search for “Bridgerton” and land on this screen: If this sounds familiar, you already know what a synopsis is — it’s a short glimpse into what a viewer can expect to see in a show. We see two types of synopses here: a series-level synopsis describing the overarching plot, and multiple episode-level synopses describing each episode. A synopsis plays a very important role for us — it helps viewers decide whether a title is worth watching or not. Every synopsis needs to strike a balance: sharing just enough to give viewers a sense of what to expect, while leaving enough intrigue to draw them in. But of course, we can’t just write anything . “In the fog-drenched streets of Victorian London, Detective Daphne Bridgerton races to unmask a serial killer known only as the elusive Lady Whistledown.” Intriguing? Definitely. But it is most certainly not the premise of Bridgerton. Which leads us to the first (and most important) rule of writing a good synopsis: it must be factual . At Netflix’s scale, with thousands of titles, multiple episodes per season and multiple languages, fact-checking all of these by hand simply doesn’t scale. This is where our factuality service comes in: an automated way to judge whether a synopsis is factual or not. Our current factuality checker feeds a reasoning model everything we know about a title (like metadata and text assets) and asks it to judge synopsis factuality according to a rigorous rubric. There are two main limitations of this approach that we want to optimize: High cost of long-context reasoning calls: Each decision requires expensive, long-context model calls to reasoning models, which doesn’t scale well when we want to check multiple titles, episodes, languages, and style variants. Misaligned rationales: The model’s explanations often diverge from our annotators’ reasoning, which makes its factuality verdicts less reliable. We want these rationales to be better aligned so that (1) the model can consistently flag nuanced errors, and (2) its explanations can be used downstream to automatically correct issues in the synopsis. Our new approach tackles both problems at once. On the cost side, it delivers a 52.4% reduction per synopsis. On the quality side, it significantly improves both verdict accuracy and reasoning alignment: Recall–Fail ( “Of all truly non-factual synopses, how many does the system correctly reject?” ) rises from 0.77 to 0.86 , and the new factuality service’s explanations now show ~ 82% overlap with human rationales (up from ~ 69% ). In other words, it’s not just cheaper and more accurate — it’s also much better aligned with how our expert annotators actually judge synopses. So, what exactly does factuality mean? Let’s go back to the Bridgerton example. Why AI Agents Are Repeating 2019’s Microservices Mistake
abstract: Microservices changed how we build software by breaking large applications into smaller, independently deployable services. That made systems easier to develop and scale, but it introduced a different class of problems: The behavior of the whole system got harder to see. AI agents are now following a similar path. A workflow that once lived inside a single application gets split across several agents, each responsible for one task. Individual pieces may work exactly as designed while the overall workflow gradually produces worse results. The difference is that agents make these systems far faster and cheaper to create, which makes it easier to repeat the same architectural mistake at a much larger scale. I learned this the hard way. My name was on the design doc. Splitting that workflow across three agents was a reasonable call, and I would still defend most of the reasoning. But if you’d asked me that afternoon how we would find out when the thing quietly stopped working, I had no answer. Months later, in a quality review, a reviewer noticed something felt off before any of our instrumentation caught it. Latency looked fine, error rates were flat, and every service in the chain returned what it was supposed to return. What we had was a slow decline in output quality, and it took about three weeks to trace. The first agent handed a set of documents to the next one for summarization. The summarizer dropped a field it had judged to be a low signal. A downstream agent then made a confident recommendation without that field. Every agent did what it had been designed to do, and the result was still wrong. I should have anticipated it, because I’d been on the product side through the microservices years and had seen this pattern before. The hangover we already paid for Breaking down monoliths was a good decision for most teams, but one thing was forgotten. Decomposition did not make the difficult parts of the system disappear. It moved them into the gaps between services, where the people accountable for the overall product could no longer see them. The bill landed around 2019, and it landed on the delivery schedule rather than the incident channel. Teams were running hundreds of services with limited tracing and no contract versioning, and the real symptom was slower delivery. Shipping took longer than before, because engineers spent their weeks picking through those services. Agents are running the same arc faster, because standing one up takes an afternoon and a prompt instead of a repo and a deploy pipeline. When creating an agent is that cheap, product teams make agents without asking anyone, and nobody keeps track of what the agents are and what they’re doing. Service sprawl at least showed up in your Kubernetes manifests. Agents get created inside product surfaces and workflow tools, and inside somebody’s weekend automation of their own job. title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
abstract: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid. One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables). The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport . Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity. Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out. Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand. The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company. Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
abstract: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy. I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control. “It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.” Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation. Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry , but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth. “Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.” Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator. He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what’s going on,” he says. title: Innovating with AI in the special chemicals industry
abstract: As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market. For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance. Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams. Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work. Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments. But, Rao emphasizes, “it’s not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.” Scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively. By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust. “Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they’re about to create,” Rao says, “things go a lot better.” Cloud infrastructure also gives the company flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers. These capabilities could prove especially valuable in advancing sustainability. Digital modeling can help researchers evaluate more formulations, explore materials such as starch and corn-based alternatives, and assess trade-offs across a product’s life cycle. Promising a material in a laboratory is only the first step. Scaling production while meeting performance expectations, regulatory requirements, and financial constraints is still a tightrope walk, but AI’s ability to model multiple variables could help teams navigate those competing demands. Looking to the future, Rao expects AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins, and connected data to converge as laboratories become more intelligent and manufacturing plants more efficient. The opportunity, he suggests, lies in bringing these capabilities together responsibly and at scale. “It’s not just a single technology. I think it’s the combination of all of these, and it’ll be the ability to connect all these processes that are going to generate tremendous amounts of data.” This webcast is produced in partnership with Infosys. title: The climate case for AI has not been made
abstract: This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic likely to dominate the conversation is artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action. But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet, despite some very optimistic claims from AI companies. In 2024, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman declared that AI would unleash “astounding triumphs,” including “fixing the climate.” The year before, in a 2023 op-ed , the head of sustainability at Google and her coauthor wrote that AI could reduce global emissions 5% to 10% by 2030. Some academic researchers have examined these AI-related climate claims. A peer-reviewed study published last year, led by researchers at the London School of Economics’ Grantham Research Institute and the firm Systemiq, estimated that AI could help cut global emissions by the equivalent of 3.2 to 5.4 billion tons of carbon dioxide annually by 2035—roughly on par with the US’s annual energy-related emissions on the high end, even after subtracting AI’s own energy footprint. Those potential gains are mostly concentrated in three sectors: power, meat and dairy, and vehicles. But projections like these are only as good as our willingness to test them against present-day reality. So is there evidence that the largest companies in these three sectors are beginning to integrate AI in line with the study’s projections, and if so, do the results match expectations? Or is the 2035 number still mostly aspirational? Companies across these sectors have announced plenty of initial efforts to incorporate AI into various business practices. But an AI-assisted review of public information from significant market actors in each sector, conducted and reviewed by the second author of this piece, found that few have announced they’re pursuing the specific emissions-reducing routes that informed the projections in the study—and fewer still claim they’ve used them to achieve meaningful climate progress. The power sector is where the earlier study’s underlying math is most concrete: AI-driven forecasting of supply and demand could increase the amount of renewable electricity that reaches the grid from already-built solar and wind facilities by up to 20%, which could prevent an estimated 1.8 billion tons of emissions a year. Yet of the grid operators reviewed in China, the United States, and Europe, only one deployed a known meaningful, working AI program of this sort, according to the analysis. A partnership between the UK’s National Grid ESO and Open Climate Fix halved the grid operator’s solar-forecast error (the difference between the amount of incoming sunlight predicted and the amount that actually reaches solar panels), avoiding hundreds of thousands of tons of carbon dioxide a year. Beyond this example in the UK, though, many other grid operators in the EU, the US, and China had little to show in the public record in terms of the AI integration envisioned by the study. The meat and dairy sector offers the starkest contrast between technology readiness and market reality. To achieve the 2035 emission reductions anticipated in the earlier study, AI would need to close the taste and cost gap between traditional proteins and alternative ones, such as lab-grown or plant-based burgers and milk substitutes. In one of the clearest efforts to achieve this, the AI and food tech company NotCo recently formed a joint venture with Kraft Heinz using its platform Giuseppe , which analyzes plant molecular data to pinpoint combinations replicating the taste, texture, and smell of animal products. abstract: This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast . Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance. However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof? There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP? Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution. title: DCU shake-up: James Gunn and Peter Safran out post-merger
abstract: It's barely been two months since the controversial Paramount and Warner Bros. merger, and we've already got a shockingly unexpected ouster : Co-CEOs of the rebooted DC Universe, James Gunn and Peter Safran, are stepping down from that role despite the Hollywood rumor mill assuming that the duo would be safe. It's unclear whether the pair chose to resign or were forced out, or what will happen to their planned slate of projects beyond 2028's Superman: Man of Tomorrow , which is in post-production. Producer Jeremy Latcham—a protege of Marvel's Kevin Feige who worked with Gunn on Guardians of the Galaxy among other MCU films—will replace them. Per Gunn and Safran's joint statement : Four years ago, we set out to unite DC under one creative vision. In that time, we helped restore Superman to the heart of DC, while opening new doors and telling new stories in film and television with Peacemaker , Creature Commandos, Lanterns and Clayface. We’re immensely proud of the team that turned that ambition into something real, including the actors, crews and executives we had the opportunity to collaborate with. We’ve shared a creative history with Jeremy going back to Marvel, and we’re eager to see the perspective he brings to DC’s next chapter. We’re excited to return to what drew us to this job in the first place, which is telling the stories we love, including the next chapter of Clark and Lex’s journey in Man of Tomorrow . DCU fans are mourning the news and what it could mean for the franchise. My feelings are mixed. On the one hand, I'm on record that I’ve found the rebooted DC Universe films released thus far to be enjoyable but rather forgettable, even when the positives outweigh the negatives . (I have yet to see Clayface , which debuted to good reviews and a solid box office showing.) But HBO has done right by the DCU: I loved both seasons of Peacemaker; Lanterns is a shining beacon of what is possible when someone is allowed to get really creative within the genre; and I'm very much looking forward to next year's Jimmy Olsen (Skylar Gisondo) series The People v. Gorilla Grodd —described as a “mockumentary crime comedy superhero series.” Read full article Comments

title: Man who lost $308,000 on sports bets sues Kalshi for offering illegal gambling
abstract: A man who lost over $308,000 making sports wagers on Kalshi is suing the prediction market for violating the state of Washington's ban on online gambling. He's trying to turn those losses into an overall victory with a lawsuit seeking a payment of over $580,000. Bellevue, Washington, resident Scott Bright's "wagering occurred at a time when it was unlawful in Washington and when the Washington Attorney General had already sued KalshiEX LLC in this Court alleging precisely that," said the gambler's lawsuit filed on September 24 in King County Superior Court. Kalshi has since filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit. While state attorneys general throughout the US are trying to shut down Kalshi for allegedly violating state gambling laws, Bright's case tests whether unsuccessful gamblers can obtain restitution from the company through individual lawsuits. title: A Sam Altman parody offers an amusing lesson in memory management
abstract: Sam Altman's recent comments on the Cheeky Pint podcast inspired developer Iain Kay to create a satirical script that allows users to email the OpenAI CEO once per day if more than 10 percent of their system RAM is reported as available. Ram-Altman is described by its creator as a "parody project" launched in response to Altman's viral remarks about RAM in your personal PC. As reported by The Verge , on the October 29 episode recorded with Stripe President John Collison, Altman said, "A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open source models, we’re going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center. But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5 percent of the time." Altman has since explained that his comments were taken out of context and briefly changed his display name to "RAM Altman" on X, which Kay calls on the project GitHub, "objectively excellent and where the project gets its name." title: Vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices is under active exploitation
abstract: Hackers are actively exploiting a recently discovered critical vulnerability that allows them to log in to privileged accounts on many Linux systems, multiple researchers are reporting. The vulnerability, tracked under the name *sshole, arises from the interaction between OpenSSH and a code library known as musl. Linux systems that use both of these packages and meet certain other requirements can be hacked to give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts in a matter of seconds. *sshole became publicly known last Thursday and quickly stoked concerns it could lead to widespread compromise of Linux machines. Four days later, the prediction shows signs of becoming real. Attackers conducting "mature intrusions" Security firm Greynoise said Monday that honeypots it maintains in Southeast Asia have come under attack by a group it’s tracking as GT10. The group conducted “mature intrusions" into the systems, which Greynoise uses to detect attempted or successful attacks in real time. Greynoise subsequently gained access to a GT10 server that revealed potential other victims and some of the tools used in the campaign. A backdoor the group is using in the attacks contains Chinese language comments and appears to be generated with the use of AI. Read full article Comments

title: Pentagon mulls placing fleet of military satellites around the Moon
abstract: The US military has published a Request for Information on a federal procurement website signaling interest in deploying a "proliferated cislunar constellation" consisting of an unspecified number of satellites performing an undisclosed mission in the vicinity of the Moon. The announcement follows statements in recent months from the Space Force's acquisitions chief for advanced programs, Maj. Gen. Stephen Purdy, that the military was getting serious about extending its reach to the Moon. The Space Force's most distant satellites today are in geostationary orbit, some 22,000 miles (36,000 kilometers) over the equator, collecting routine surveillance and missile warning data. Most recently, Purdy spoke of a shift in Pentagon leadership's thinking about the Moon following an executive order signed by President Donald Trump last December. The order set out the Trump administration's space policy. One section of the order deals with the US government's ability to detect, characterize, and counter threats to US space interests from low-Earth orbit to cislunar space, the term of art for the region of space around the Moon. title: Claude Code is accidentally exposing secrets all over GitHub
abstract: Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That's the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who discovered thousands of secrets , including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories. The leak stems from the way Claude Code handles user approval for automated shell commands. When a user chooses the "Yes, and don't ask again" option to approve running a command, that choice gets stored as part of a rule in the local ".claude/settings.local.json" file on the user's computer. That rule is sometimes coded as a pattern, but the command itself is often written to that settings file as is, including any sensitive information that may be embedded within it. This isn't really a significant security issue if the settings file stays on the user's local machine (assuming that machine doesn't become compromised itself, of course). And Anthropic notes in its Claude Code documentation that this particular settings file gets added to the developer's global .gitignore list , which usually prevents it from being shared publicly. title: SpaceX now fundamentally an "infrastructure company," senior official says
abstract: For a long time, SpaceX has been synonymous with the development of newer, larger, and ever-more-reusable rockets. But that began to change over the last decade with the introduction of Starlink, and the change has accelerated during the last 18 months as the company has pivoted to data and artificial intelligence. At last week's UP.Summit conference in Florida, the vice president of launch at SpaceX, Kiko Dontchev, offered some of the most revealing comments to date about the company's changing focus, how it is embracing AI, and why the Falcon 9 rocket—which has dominated global launch for a decade and remains the world's preeminent launch vehicle—is firmly on the road to retirement. "In the last couple years, when I talk about SpaceX, yes, we are a rocket company, but fundamentally we are an infrastructure company at this point," Dontchev said. "We're building infrastructure on the ground and low Earth orbit, soon on the Moon, and obviously eventually Mars." Read full article Comments

title: F1 in Brazil: You’ve got to keep your tires alive
abstract: In sports, a “ dead rubber ” is a match that takes place after the outcome of the series or championship has already been decided. The people in charge hate this*—if you wrap up a title two-thirds of the way through a season, the viewers evaporate, as there’s nothing left at stake. But anyone who decided to skip this year’s Brazilian Grand Prix this past weekend missed one of the year’s most entertaining races, as a combination of a mixed-up starting order, some very fast drivers at the back, and a wet track that dried and then saw rain again resulted in action aplenty. A peculiarity of F1 is that even if you manage to win a championship, there’s no guarantee you’ll be in a position to defend it. Take McLaren’s Lando Norris, who took the crown in 2025 after a nail-biting fight with his teammate Oscar Piastri and Red Bull’s Max Verstappen. Sadly for Lando, McLaren did not start this year in a position to win races, and even with several upgrades, the team has produced a car that is still very tricky to drive. But this weekend in Brazil, Norris demonstrated the form that earned him the number 1. Rain on Saturday during qualifying helped jumble the usual running order. It was heavy enough that drivers used the wet weather tire with deep treads, which usually generates so much spray that visibility disappears and running has to be suspended. But with fewer cars on track in the later knockout qualifying sessions, this was not a problem for once. More disruption came from grid penalties for Verstappen and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, both of whom needed to use extra power unit components outside of the season’s allowance. title: New Democratic Congress will likely strip the gilding from Trump's Golden Dome
abstract: Two of the top lawmakers backing the Pentagon's Golden Dome missile defense shield are among the wave of Republicans leaving Congress in the coming Democratic takeover, raising questions about the future of President Donald Trump's signature second-term defense initiative. The shakeup on Capitol Hill comes after military officials signaled in recent months that they might backpedal from one element Trump asked for in Golden Dome: the capability to shoot down missiles in their initial boost phase shortly after launch. The Golden Dome has escaped serious congressional scrutiny since Trump announced the program in January 2025, one week into his second term in the White House. That lack of scrutiny will change as Democrats take responsibility for writing the Pentagon's budget, introduce limits on funding, and put forth bills to strip out Golden Dome's most controversial component and give the program a new name. title: Physicists listened to electrical noise to crack a superconductor mystery
abstract: Superconductors carry electricity without resistance, but most only work a few degrees above absolute zero. In the late 1980s, copper-based materials called cuprates were found to superconduct at higher temperatures—reachable with affordable liquid nitrogen. Yet nearly 40 years later, physicists still don't agree on why. In a recent Science study, a team of physicists led by Milan Allan of Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and Ingmar Swart of Utrecht University in the Netherlands has found some answers by listening to the faint electrical crackle of current flowing into a cuprate. The missing electrons Central to the mystery of cuprates’ high-temperature superconductivity is a strange state called the pseudogap. “The pseudogap is a phenomenon of missing electrons,” Allan said. Above the temperature at which cuprates become superconducting, some of their electrons seem to vanish—measurements find far fewer of them at the energies where they should be. “Everybody knows that from different probes, you see that there's these vanishing electrons, but nobody knows why,” Allan said. title: The Bantu expansion changed Africa. Scientists are still tracing how.
abstract: It’s not easy to extract iron from its ore. But the peoples of the ancient city of Great Zimbabwe—the capital of a thriving kingdom in southern Africa between 1000 to 1700 AD—were masters. At sites near the city’s stone ruins, clusters of iron-smelting furnaces survive today as mounds of rubble. At Mashava, a village 25 miles northwest, fragments bear fingermarks of those who long ago smoothed the structures’ clay interiors. Some of the furnaces were nearly an adult’s arm span in width, with walls thick and strong to contain the heat of more than 2,100° Fahrenheit needed to smelt iron. Unlike other furnaces that required workers to force air into them with bellows, these were designed to suck air in, then out through a chimney, no human labor required. This would have made it significantly easier to produce the iron, which was fashioned into hoes, axes, and arrowheads. Read full article Comments

title: British soldier ignored order to pull his SIM card, then got blackmailed
abstract: An Estonian newspaper recently revealed that a British soldier disobeyed a direct order to remove the SIM card from his cellphone before being deployed to a part of Estonia, approximately 90 miles west of the Russian border. As a result of his refusal to engage in this element of operational security (opsec), the soldier, Daniel Barton-Kennedy, had his phone hacked, and nude photos of himself were stolen and used as blackmail against him. Eventually, Barton-Kennedy was court-martialed for disobeying a lawful command, pled guilty, was reduced in rank, and ordered to serve 10 months in detention. Read full article Comments

title: TASTE, 토스의 추천 파운데이션 플랫폼
abstract: 금융 상품에 관심이 있는 사람을 찾는 모델, 푸시를 클릭할 사람을 찾는 모델, 좋아할 미니앱을 추천하는 모델. 풀어야 할 문제는 다르지만, 이해해야 하는 대상은 모두 같은 토스의 사용자입니다. 토스에 쌓이는 방대하고 서로 다른 데이터를 충분히 학습하여 배운 내용을 여러 추천 문제에 활용할 수는 없을까요? TASTE(Toss Automated Standard Targeting Engine) 는 이 질문에서 시작했습니다. 사용자의 다양한 행동을 함께 예측하고, 그 과정에서 배운 ‘사용자 표현’을 다른 서비스 모델에 전달하고자 했습니다. 여러 서비스의 온오프라인 실험에서 이 표현이 예측에 도움이 된다는 것까지 확인했습니다. 이 글에서는 여러 행동을 함께 학습하고, 그 과정에서 얻은 사용자 표현을 다른 추천 모델에 전달하며, 이를 다시 개선하는 과정 을 소개합니다. 한 번 배운 사용자 정보를 여러 추천 문제에 활용하는 것, 이것이 저희가 생각하는 추천 파운데이션 모델의 출발점입니다. 같은 사용자를 모델마다 다시 배우고 있었습니다 토스에는 금융중개, 광고, 쇼핑, 결제, Apps in Toss 등 여러 서비스가 있습니다. 서비스가 늘어날수록 클릭, 구매, 전환 등을 예측하는 모델도 늘어납니다. 모델마다 목표는 달라도 사용하는 사용자 정보는 겹치는 부분이 많습니다. 나이와 같은 속성, 앱에서 이용한 기능, 소비 이력 등이 대표적입니다. 각 모델은 이 정보를 자신의 예측에 필요한 형태로 가공하고 학습합니다. 같은 정보를 모델마다 따로 준비하고 학습하면서 중복 작업이 생겼습니다. 데이터를 충분히 활용하는 일도 쉽지 않았습니다. 토스는 월간 활성 사용자(MAU)가 2천만 명을 넘어, 주요 서버 로그만 해도 하루에 수십억 건 이상 쌓입니다. 사용자 한 명을 이해하기 위해 살펴봐야 할 정보도 방대합니다. 데이터의 성격도 제각각입니다. 마이데이터는 수십 개의 API를 통해 들어오며, 데이터마다 수집 시점과 정보를 확보할 수 있는 사용자 범위가 다릅니다. 외부 앱 이용 정보를 담은 MMP 데이터는 이벤트가 지나치게 많거나, 반대로 너무 적기도 합니다. 서버 로그와 마이데이터, MMP 데이터는 활용하고 분석할 수 있는 동의 조건도 모두 다릅니다. 결국 각 모델은 예측 문제를 풀기에 앞서, 이 방대하고 서로 다른 데이터를 어떻게 모으고 학습할지부터 해결해야 했습니다. 서비스별 예측 모델은 응답 시간 등 서비스가 요구하는 수준(SLA)을 맞춰야 해서 상대적으로 크기가 작습니다. 이런 제약 아래에서 개별 모델이 방대한 정보를 충분히 학습하기는 쉽지 않습니다. 그래서 서비스 중인 모델들이 예측에 도움이 되는 사용자 정보를 놓치고 있을 수 있다는 가설을 세웠습니다. 모델을 합치는 것만으로는 성능이 좋아지지 않았습니다 “ 여러 모델에 필요한 사용자 표현을 한 번에 학습하고, 그 결과를 여러 목적에 활용할 수 있을까? ” 먼저 주요 앱이벤트를 동시에 예측하는 멀티태스크 학습을 시도했습니다. 사용자 정보를 예측에 필요한 표현으로 바꾸는 인코더(Encoder)를 공유하고, 그 뒤에 결제나 특정 서비스 이용 등 과제별 예측을 담당하는 헤드(Head)를 붙이는 방식입니다. 같은 정보를 받아도 과제마다 필요한 부분은 다릅니다. 과제별로 필요한 정보를 다르게 조합할 수 있도록, 처음에는 MMoE(Multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts) 구조를 시도했습니다. 빠르게 가능성을 살펴보기 위해 초기에는 학습 사용자를 100만 명으로 줄였습니다. 사용자 수를 줄인 영향을 살펴볼 수 있도록, 기존 모델에 사용하던 LightGBM도 100만 명 규모로 학습했습니다. 같은 사용자 수로 학습한 두 모델을 비교했을 때, MMoE의 성능(AUROC)은 과제별로 따로 학습한 LightGBM보다 낮았습니다. 이 결과만으로는 여러 과제를 함께 학습하는 방식의 이점을 확인하기 어려웠습니다. 학습 데이터와 모델을 확장하자 성능이 올랐습니다 하지만 저희는 다른 가설을 세웠습니다. “ 한 모델이 여러 행동을 동시에 예측하려면, 각 행동을 따로 학습할 때보다 더 많은 데이터가 필요한 것 아닐까? ” 공동학습 자체의 한계로 결론짓기 전에, 더 많은 사용자와 더 풍부한 행동 정보를 학습해보기로 했습니다. 우선 학습 대상을 100만 명에서 학습에 사용할 수 있는 전체 사용자로 넓혔습니다. 사용자 요약 정보도 기존 1,000여 개에서 2,000개 이상으로 늘렸습니다. 요약 정보에 담기지 않은 행동의 흐름도 배울 수 있도록, 최근 앱이벤트 시퀀스를 Causal Transformer로 읽고 압축했습니다. 늘어난 입력에 맞춰 모델 구조도 개선했습니다. 요약 정보를 처리하는 인코더에는 DCN-V2를, 과제별 예측을 담당하는 부분에는 PLE(Progressive Layered Extraction)를 사용했습니다. 학습 사용자 규모와 입력 피처, 모델 구조를 확대한 뒤에는 기존 모델의 성능을 넘어설 수 있었습니다. 공통 앱이벤트 예측에서 Macro Recall@5k의 상대 개선율은 약 35.1%입니다. 초기의 낮은 성능을 공동학습의 한계로 받아들이지 않고 가설을 세워 실험한 결과입니다. 사용자 요약 정보를 2,000개 이상 사용하면서 새로운 의문도 생겼습니다. 요약 정보가 충분하다면 시퀀스 모듈은 없어도 되지 않을까요? 이를 확인하기 위해 시퀀스 모듈을 제거한 별도 실험을 진행했고, Macro Recall@5k가 상대적으로 7.6% 낮아지는 것을 확인했습니다. 많은 요약 정보를 사용하더라도, 시퀀스를 직접 학습하면 예측에 도움이 된다는 정보를 추가로 얻었습니다. 소비까지 함께 배우며 목적에 맞는 구조를 찾았습니다 앱이벤트 공동학습의 성과를 바탕으로, 주요 소비 이벤트까지 학습 범위를 넓혔습니다. 앱이벤트 시퀀스가 요약 정보를 보완했던 것처럼, 소비도 이력을 직접 학습하면 도움이 될 것이라고 생각했습니다. 그래서 미래 소비를 예측하는 과제와 함께, 브랜드·카테고리 등의 소비 시퀀스를 읽는 인코더를 추가했습니다. 하지만 한 모델에서 모두 학습하자 과제별 성과가 달라졌습니다. 소비 예측은 기존 개별 모델보다 좋아졌지만, 앱이벤트의 Macro Recall@5k는 앱이벤트만 한 번에 학습했을 때보다 낮아졌습니다. 앱이벤트와 소비는 행동의 성격도, 정답 데이터가 들어오는 시점도 크게 달랐습니다. 두 목적을 예측하는 데 필요한 표현과 학습 방식도 다를 수 있었습니다. 그래서 각 목적에 맞는 표현을 따로 학습하면 성능을 개선할 수 있을 것 이라는 가설을 세웠습니다. 입력 정보는 함께 활용하되, 앱이벤트와 소비를 예측하는 모델은 인코더부터 따로 학습했습니다. 두 모델 모두 앱이벤트 이력, 소비 이력, 사용자 요약 정보를 받으며, 각 모델 안에서는 여전히 여러 앱이벤트 또는 소비 과제를 함께 학습합니다. 모델별로 구조를 탐색하고 최적화해, 각 목적에 맞는 학습 방식을 찾았습니다. 목적을 나누고 각 모델의 구조와 학습 방법을 개선한 결과, 앱이벤트의 Macro Recall@5k는 단일 모델 TASTE보다 8.7% 높아졌습니다. 소비 예측은 같은 지표에서 기존 모델 대비 브랜드 33.9%, 중분류 111%, 소분류 65.8% 개선됐습니다. 여러 과제를 함께 학습하는 이점을 살리면서도, 목적에 맞게 모델을 나누고 최적화해 각 서비스에 필요한 성능을 확보할 수 있었습니다. 학습한 모델을 실제 운영에 연결했습니다 TASTE가 제공하는 결과물은 크게 두 가지입니다. 하나는 모델이 직접 계산한 행동별 예측 확률이고, 다른 하나는 학습한 사용자 정보를 담은 임베딩입니다. 먼저 예측 확률을 실제 운영에 활용한 사례를 소개하겠습니다. 우선 여러 과제를 함께 학습하면서 개별 모델마다 반복하던 데이터 준비·학습·추론 작업을 통합하고, 중복되는 인프라 사용과 운영 부담을 줄였습니다. 이렇게 생성한 확률값은 목표 행동을 할 가능성이 높은 사용자를 찾는 데 활용했습니다. 토스에서 IM(Intelligence Manager)은 홈 상단 배너를 노출하고 푸시, SMS·LMS, 브랜드톡을 발송하는 통합 메시지 발송 허브입니다. 캠페인 담당자가 많은 시간을 쓰는 일 중 하나는 ‘누구에게 보낼까’를 정하는 것이었습니다. 같은 푸시라도 목표에 따라 어떤 행동 이

title: CoupledFlow: One-Step Neural Operators for Coupled Multi-Physics PDEs
abstract: This paper introduces COUPLED FLOW, a new neural operator learning framework for multi-physics PDE systems that captures the co-evolution of multiple physical processes by modeling their cross-process interactions. Unlike existing neural operator methods that primarily target single-physics settings, COUPLED FLOW employs a novel structure-constrained flow matching algorithm to learn process- specific mean velocity fields conditioned on the full multi-physics state. This enables fast and accurate one-step prediction of coupled PDE systems that would otherwise require expensive numerical simulations. A key challenge in training COUPLED FLOW however lies in sampling structure-constrained conditional flow interpolants that capture cross-process correlations and serve as training examples for flow matching. To address this challenge, we derive a multi-physics mean-flow consistency identity that characterizes cross-process interactions and defines the structure-constrained mean-flow matching loss. To provide informative training samples for flow matching with this loss, we develop a principled method for sampling correlated conditional interpolants based on posterior multi-output Gaus- sian processes, which capture richer cross-process correlations than the commonly used endpoint-conditioned linear interpolants. We also establish a theoretical re- sult showing that the Wasserstein-2 distance between the predicted and oracle PDE solution distributions is upper-bounded in terms of the structure-constrained flow matching loss and the smoothness of the learned flow. Experiments across diverse coupled PDE benchmarks demonstrate that COUPLED FLOW consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art neural operators and generative PDE solvers.

title: Can small transformers learn the language of Coxeter groups?
abstract: The field of mechanistic interpretability is well-suited to collaborative projects between mathematicians and AI researchers. This work describes one such project. We trained a small transformer to learn the language of the Coxeter group affine A2, best known as the symmetries of the tiling of the Euclidean plane by equilateral triangles. We then formulated and proved a word-theoretic conjecture about affine A2 after observing the attention patterns of the trained model.

title: Optimal Byzantine-resilient Federated Learning with User-level Differential Privacy
abstract: Real-world deployment of federated learning (FL) requires resilience against adversarial clients and data privacy. Byzantine fault captures the worst-case behavior of adversarial clients, while differential privacy (DP) provides statistical guarantees against privacy loss. In particular, user-level DP guards a client's entire contribution and provides more realistic protection against information leakage. Despite intensive efforts, the minimax-optimal convergence bound of Byzantine-resilient FL with user-level DP remains open. We establish an information-theoretic lower bound for any Byzantine-resilient empirical risk minimization problem under user-level DP and heterogeneous clients. We propose ByzULDP, a central DP algorithm featuring a two-level momentum across the client and server. Client-side momentum mitigates stochastic gradient variance during robust aggregation. Unlike the fault-free case, naively combining non-linear Byzantine-resilient aggregation with central DP noise can be insufficient to guarantee convergence to a bounded neighborhood of a stationary point. Our key contribution is a server-side momentum that leverages a property specific to user-level DP, where privacy sensitivity depends on how client updates are constructed, to empower convergence. ByzULDP achieves the order-optimal convergence bound for strongly-convex objectives, with vanishing error terms decaying at the optimal $O(1/T)$ and $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ rates for strongly-convex and non-convex objectives, respectively. We corroborate our analysis with numerical experiments on real-world datasets across diverse privacy budgets.

title: Robust Satisficing Ensemble: Scalable Model Aggregation Under Distribution Shifts
abstract: Standard ensemble methods can improve robustness by mitigating individual model stochasticity, but they frequently fail to generalize beyond the training distribution, leaving systems vulnerable to out-of-distribution (OOD) data. We introduce the Robust Satisficing Ensemble (RSE), a scalable probabilistic aggregation framework designed to secure model combinations by minimizing their fragility against distributional changes. By bridging a robust satisficing objective with a quadratic risk surrogate, RSE derives an analytical inner adversary. This fundamental reformulation enables highly efficient weight updates without the computational bottleneck of standard minimax optimization, crucially decoupling optimization complexity from sample size to scale effectively to large datasets. In particular, we prove a geometrically decaying truncation error for the fragility approximation via Lagrange-Burmann expansion and establish stationarity guarantees for RSE. We evaluate RSE across a comprehensive spectrum of distribution shifts, including adversarial label shift (SST-5, TREC), natural subpopulation and temporal shifts (CivilComments, HuffPost). Our results demonstrate that RSE consistently outperforms strong robust baselines, including GroupDRO, IRM, and SRM. These findings establish RSE as a practical, theoretically grounded safeguard for reliable model aggregation in dynamic environments.

title: Approximate Recall, Approximate Forecasts: Recall as a Diagnostic for LLM Forecasting Errors
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit approximate recall: they retain coarse associations about past events while losing fidelity on specific details. Past research on LLMs has quantified different models' forecasting ability in real-world events using prediction markets, but has not studied how losing said fidelity impacts their forecasting abilities. For example: while an LLM correctly recalls that the answer to: ''Did Anna Sawai win the Best Drama Actress in the 76th Emmy Awards?'' is ''Yes,'' it incorrectly states the event date as September 22 rather than September 15. In this paper, we introduce a novel metric called the Recall Fidelity Score to study how imprecision in internalized knowledge propagates to forecasting capability on future events. On resolved historical markets, we find that higher local recall fidelity around semantically similar past events predicts lower forecasting error on resolved markets, and the same signal predicts smaller distance from open markets prices.

title: Robust and Efficient Continual Model Merging via Global Singular Subspace Separation and Restoration
abstract: Continual model merging incrementally integrates task-specific models without revisiting past models or data. However, repeated merging entangles past task components and distorts their singular geometry, making balanced task-wise allocation increasingly difficult. We propose Global Singular Subspace Separation and Restoration (GS3R), which augments the merged update with a compact restoration state. At each merge, GS3R restores the retained singular geometry, separates task-wise subspaces, and globally reallocates the available rank across tasks fairly. To reduce merging-time memory overhead, we further introduce Pre-merge Restoration and Flushing (PRF). Experiments on vision, NLP, and multimodal benchmarks show that GS3R provides a strong accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

title: Online Imitation Learning for Stabilizing Vlasov--Poisson Plasmas
abstract: We study the problem of controlling instability in the Vlasov--Poisson plasma systems, a fundamental challenge for nuclear fusion control. Motivated by the partial observability of plasma states in practice, we investigate imitation learning algorithms that learn from a fully-observable expert controller, but operate under macroscopic measurements. We theoretically establish a separation between online and offline imitation learning --- even a small behavior cloning error leads to error compounding that exponentially amplifies instability over time. By way of contrast, the online imitation learning loss can polynomially control the stability of rollout trajectories. We then propose a DAgger-style algorithm that learns the stabilizing controller under partial observability. Simulation results on a 1D Vlasov--Poisson system demonstrate that our algorithm can effectively stabilize plasma instabilities over longer time horizons than behavior cloning.

title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Deleting Weights in LLM Post-Training
abstract: How little of a pretrained large language model (LLM) has to change for it to acquire new capabilities? We find that zeroing fewer than 0.05% of its weights, with no other modification, matches full fine-tuning (FFT) at scale across three LLM post-training regimes: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, supervised fine-tuning, and on-policy distillation. Our method, Deletion Tuning, learns a binary mask over the gate projection of transformer blocks. Two practical advantages follow: the trained mask is hundreds to thousands of times smaller than the corresponding FFT checkpoint, and Deletion Tuning forgets far less, which addresses a central challenge in continual learning. Under reinforcement learning, its prior-task accuracy stays near the base level while FFT, LoRA, and random sparse fine-tuning lose up to 5.4 points. To understand why masking alone suffices, we analyze the geometry of the learned weight changes under reinforcement learning using stable rank, spectrum drift, and principal-weight overlap. Compared with LoRA and random sparse fine-tuning, Deletion Tuning is closest to FFT across the three measures.

title: SWXAI: A Unified Multimodal Explainability Library for Space Weather Forecasting and Heliophysics
abstract: Space weather forecasting and heliophysics increasingly rely on machine learning models that process heterogeneous inputs such as multi-viewpoint multi-wavelength solar images and rasters, multivariate time series, spatial annotations, and tabular event-level data. However, explainability workflows remain fragmented across libraries, model interfaces, and output formats, limiting reuse and reproducibility. We present SWXAI, an open-source library that unifies explainable AI (XAI) workflows for image, time-series, and tabular data in space weather forecasting and heliophysics. SWXAI provides a common, extensible interface across commonly used vision, time-series, and tabular learning models, with validation, adaptation, and persistent explanation objects. It also includes domain-grounded examples, reproducible notebooks, tests, and documentation, enabling users to inspect outputs, swap models or explainers, and extend workflows to new heliophysics datasets. SWXAI reduces modality-specific engineering overhead and supports comparable, reusable explanations across heterogeneous scientific machine learning pipelines. A benchmark against direct backend implementations shows that SWXAI substantially reduces the code users write to produce an explanation, with no practical runtime cost.

title: Structurally Separated DAG Learning with Multi-Scale Normalized Closure
abstract: Continuous DAG learning commonly enforces acyclicity through scalar functions of a weighted adjacency that aggregate evidence from weighted closed walks. We add a complementary layer: matrix-valued closure logits---explicit multi-hop structural relation scores for each ordered pair---supervised alongside data fit, sparsity, and a DAGMA-style barrier on the weighted adjacency. The distinction is not scalarization of the overall objective but how path evidence is represented and exposed before aggregation. SMNC (scale-normalized multi-scale closure) builds these scores on a structural gate by repeated squaring in log space and divides each scale by its path-length budget, counteracting product-style attenuation along long cycles; diagonal entries support node-wise cycle supervision and off-diagonals optional pairwise reachability cues. In the linear model, a bounded structure--magnitude factorization ties strong effective edges to strong gates; a nonlinear induced gate offers another construction with the same intent. For sufficiently strong cycles, normalized logits admit a length-independent lower bound; under a unique-active-cycle assumption, the hard final-scale readout yields a polynomial log-gate gradient factor rather than exponential product-style decay. On cue-free, unstandardized Gaussian linear and nonlinear ER benchmarks, these models improve over DAGMA, run with default hyperparameters at a reduced budget, on denser graphs and are close to it on sparse ones.
